## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Kalaṇḍukajātaka* (Ja 127) is a narrative belonging to the Jātaka collection in the Pali Canon [SuttaCentral]. Set at Jetavana, the story was delivered by the Buddha regarding a boastful monk (*vikatthika bhikkhu*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. As noted in the commentary, both the present and past frames of the story closely parallel those of the preceding *Kaṭāhakajātaka* [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877].
According to the narrative, a slave named Kalaṇḍuka served the merchant of Bārāṇasī (*Bārāṇasiseṭṭhi*) [Fausböll 1877]. After improperly rinsing his mouth with milk and spitting upon the head of a merchant's daughter, Kalaṇḍuka is observed and rebuked by a young parrot (*sukapotaka*), who warns him of retribution in a single verse opening *Te desā tāni vatthūni* [Fausböll 1877]. In the conclusion (*samodhāna*), the Buddha reveals that the boastful monk was Kalaṇḍuka in that previous birth, while the Buddha himself had been the merchant of Bārāṇasī [Fausböll 1877].
Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus records any external parallels or significant Pali-internal text reuse for this text [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral notes four translations across four languages [SuttaCentral].
